passages.t: Belshazzar's feast, and a hand writing on the wall
passages.happening:
‘Later, King Belshazzar held a great feast for a thousand of his nobles, and he drank wine with them’ (verse 1). Under the wine's influence he orders the gold and silver vessels brought in, the ones Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple in Jerusalem, so that he, his nobles, his wives and his concubines can drink from them (verses 2-3). ‘As they drank the wine, they praised their gods of gold and silver, bronze and iron, wood and stone’ (verse 4).

At that moment the fingers of a human hand appear and write on the plaster of the wall, near the lampstand (verse 5). The king's face goes pale, his legs give way and his knees knock together (verse 6).

He calls for his enchanters, astrologers and diviners. Whoever reads the writing and explains it will be dressed in purple, given a gold chain and made third ruler in the kingdom (verse 7). But none of them can read it or explain it (verse 8), and the king is more terrified than before (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Decades have passed since chapter 4. Belshazzar was the eldest son of Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon (556 to 539 BC). For many years he was known only from Daniel, and some scholars doubted he existed. Babylonian texts found in the nineteenth century confirmed him, and showed that he governed Babylon for about ten years while his father lived at the oasis of Tema in Arabia. That explains his offer of the third place in the kingdom: he himself was second.

The vessels taken in chapter 1 return here as the center of the offense. Drinking from the vessels of a conquered people's temple was a way of celebrating the victory of one's own gods over theirs. For Belshazzar to drink from the LORD's vessels while praising gods of metal, wood and stone was deliberate mockery.

The scene moves from noise and revelry to silence and fear. The king who held a feast for a thousand is undone by a hand he cannot read.
passages.later: Isaiah had foretold the cry, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon! All the images of her gods lie shattered on the ground!” (Isaiah 21:9). A psalm says of the proud, ‘Weighed on the scale, they go up; together they are but a vapor’ (Psalm 62:9).
passages.asks: Belshazzar made a joke of holy things at a party. Ask what you treat lightly that belongs to God. And ask what you are celebrating while something is being written on the wall.

passages.happening:
Hearing the uproar, the queen enters the banquet hall (verse 10). She tells the king not to be afraid. There is a man in his kingdom who has ‘the spirit of the holy gods in him’ (verse 11). In the days of Nebuchadnezzar he was found to have insight and wisdom, and was made chief of the magicians. He can interpret dreams, explain riddles and solve hard problems. ‘Summon Daniel, therefore, and he will give you the interpretation’ (verse 12).

Daniel is brought in. The king asks, ‘Are you Daniel, one of the exiles my father the king brought from Judah?’ (verse 13). He says he has heard of Daniel's wisdom, and repeats his offer of purple, a gold chain and the third place in the kingdom if Daniel can read the writing (verses 14-16).
passages.hearers:
The queen is probably the queen mother, since the king's wives are already at the feast. Queen mothers held real influence in ancient courts, and she remembers what the king has forgotten.

Daniel is an old man by now, and apparently forgotten at court. The king knows of him only by hearsay. He calls him one of the exiles from Judah, a reminder of who Daniel is and of where the vessels came from.

Belshazzar is called Nebuchadnezzar's son, though his father was Nabonidus. In ancient usage father and son could mean ancestor and descendant, or a king and his successor on a throne. Assyrian records call Jehu of Israel the son of Omri, though Jehu had overthrown Omri's family. Those who read Daniel as sixth-century history take the word in that sense; many critical scholars see a simplification by a later writer. Either way, the link matters: Belshazzar sat on the throne of a king whose humbling he knew.
passages.later: The same words had been spoken of Joseph in Egypt, when Pharaoh asked, ‘Can we find anyone like this man, in whom the Spirit of God abides?’ (Genesis 41:38). Nebuchadnezzar had said of Daniel, ‘the spirit of the holy gods is in you’ (Daniel 4:9).
passages.asks: The king had forgotten the one person who could help him, and someone else had to remember. Ask whose wisdom you have stopped listening to. And ask whether the faithful service of years can be forgotten by the powerful and still matter to God.

passages.happening:
Daniel answers, ‘You may keep your gifts for yourself and give your rewards to someone else’ (verse 17). Still, he will read the writing.

First he reminds the king of his father. The Most High gave Nebuchadnezzar greatness, and nations trembled before him (verses 18-19). ‘But when his heart became arrogant and his spirit was hardened with pride, he was deposed from his royal throne’ (verse 20), until he acknowledged that the Most High rules (verse 21).

‘But you his son, O Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, even though you knew all this’ (verse 22). He has exalted himself against the Lord of heaven, drunk from the vessels of his house and praised gods that cannot see or hear or understand. ‘But you have failed to glorify the God who holds in His hand your very breath and all your ways’ (verse 23).

‘Now this is the inscription that was written: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN’ (verse 25). MENE: ‘God has numbered the days of your reign and brought it to an end’ (verse 26). TEKEL: ‘you have been weighed on the scales and found deficient’ (verse 27). PERES: ‘your kingdom has been divided and given over to the Medes and Persians’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Daniel speaks very differently here from the way he spoke to Nebuchadnezzar in chapter 4. There he was troubled for the king and urged him to repent. Here he refuses the gifts and speaks sharply. Belshazzar had what Nebuchadnezzar did not: the example of a king humbled before him. He knew, and did not humble himself. The verb for humble is the one that ended chapter 4.

The writing is a riddle. MENE, TEKEL and PERES are Aramaic names for weights used in trade and money: the mina, the shekel and the half-mina. Read as nouns, the words are a list of weights, which may be why the wise men could not make sense of them. Daniel reads them as verbs: numbered, weighed, divided. And PERES sounds like the word for Persia, so the verdict and those who will carry it out are named in one word.

The picture of God weighing a person on scales was familiar in the ancient world and appears elsewhere in Scripture. The first hearers knew that the king who mocked Jerusalem's God had been weighed by him.
passages.later: Job asks for that weighing: ‘let God weigh me with honest scales, that He may know my integrity’ (Job 31:6). And Jesus told of a rich man who planned to eat and drink, and was told, ‘This very night your life will be required of you’ (Luke 12:20).
passages.asks: Belshazzar's sin was not ignorance. He knew all this. Ask what you already know that you have not let humble you. And ask what you would want to be found if you were weighed on God's scales today.

passages.happening:
Belshazzar keeps his word. Daniel is dressed in purple, given a gold chain and proclaimed third ruler in the kingdom (verse 29).

‘That very night Belshazzar king of the Chaldeans was slain’ (verse 30), ‘and Darius the Mede received the kingdom at the age of sixty-two’ (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
The story ends in two short verses, and the brevity is part of the judgment. Babylon, the head of gold in the dream of chapter 2, has fallen, and the next kingdom has come. It is the first change of empire in the book.

Babylon fell to the Persian army of Cyrus in October 539 BC. The Babylonian record says it was taken without a battle. The Greek historians Herodotus and Xenophon later reported that the city fell while its people were celebrating a festival, which fits this chapter's feast.

In the Aramaic text, verse 31 is numbered as the first verse of chapter 6. The honor Daniel is given lasts a few hours. He is proclaimed third ruler of a kingdom that ends that night.
passages.later: Jeremiah had foretold the scene: messengers running ‘to announce to the king of Babylon that his city has been captured from end to end’ (Jeremiah 51:31). And Isaiah called Babylon ‘the jewel of the kingdoms, the glory of the pride of the Chaldeans’ (Isaiah 13:19), which God would overthrow.
passages.hard:
Who was Darius the Mede?

The ‘Darius the Mede’ who receives the kingdom (verse 31) is not known from other sources. Some identify him with an official under Cyrus named in Babylonian records, either the general Ugbaru, whose army took the city, or Gubaru, whom Cyrus placed over Babylon. Others, following D. J. Wiseman, identify him with Cyrus himself, reading 6:28 as the reign of Darius, that is, of Cyrus. Many critical scholars regard him as a figure formed from traditions about the later Darius I and from the prophets' expectation that the Medes would conquer Babylon (Isaiah 13:17; Jeremiah 51:11). None of these views has won general agreement, and these notes take no side.

The chapter's point does not depend on settling it. The kingdom that mocked the LORD's vessels was numbered and ended, as he had said.
passages.asks: The honors Belshazzar gave Daniel lasted a night. Ask which honors you are working for that could end as quickly. And ask what the fall of Babylon in a night says about the powers that seem permanent in your own day.
